pr.title: gh-112075: Make PyDictKeysObject thread-safe
pr.body:
Adds locking for shared keys

<!-- gh-issue-number: gh-112075 -->
* Issue: gh-112075
<!-- /gh-issue-number -->

review_comments.body: How about adding a macro for the free-threading version and the default version?

I did similar approach at listobject: https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/114651/commits/393cbefe027440f41f9099da7c4915d0e7e8529f

See: `_Py_SET_ITEMREF `

We call dict doesn't have split values as "combined".
Please use it unless there is special reason to use special word.

review_comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -140,6 +140,31 @@ To avoid slowing down lookups on a near-full table, we resize the table when
 it's USABLE_FRACTION (currently two-thirds) full.

review_comments.body:
I think we want to use `_Py_LOCK_DONT_DETACH`. Otherwise, locking the keys object can release an outer critical section. This also means that it will be important that `LOCK_KEYS()` is essentially the "inner-most" code and that we don't call `Py_DECREF()` or similar while holding the keys lock. 


```suggestion
#define LOCK_KEYS(keys) PyMutex_LockFlags(&keys->dk_mutex, _Py_LOCK_DONT_DETACH)
```

review_comments.body: As discussed previously, I think this will be a scaling bottleneck but is fine for now.

I think we want to avoid locking the shared keys when using them to create dicts.

We're OK with a possibly stale "usable size" as long as it's no smaller than the true size. The `shared_keys_usable_size` monotonically decreases (good), but is split across two fields, which makes it a bit more complex.

We should be locking the `a` and `b` dicts, which means we should just use plain loads for `ep->me_key`.

I think this `dictkeys_decref()` call would need to be after the `UNLOCK_KEYS`.

If I understand correctly, the extra incref/decref are because `dictresize` internally will decref the keys and we don't want them to be freed until after we unlock them.

@corona10 is there a significant difference in performance between the two builds? I'm not sure if it is worth it to add these preprocessor guards everywhere if there is no measurable effect :) Is there a different motivation than performance?
Regardless of whether we do the macro approach everywhere, I think it's a good idea in this specific case (specifically for performance).

review_comments.body: I'm not sure this is correct without locking the keys. This can happen concurrently with `split_keys_entry_added()`. At a minimum, we'd need to use relaxed atomics wherever we load `keys->dk_usable` to avoid data races.

review_comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -151,9 +151,41 @@ ASSERT_DICT_LOCKED(PyObject *op)
 }
 #define ASSERT_DICT_LOCKED(op) ASSERT_DICT_LOCKED(_Py_CAST(PyObject*, op))
 
-#else
+#define LOCK_KEYS(keys) PyMutex_LockFlags(&keys->dk_mutex, _Py_LOCK_DONT_DETACH)
+#define UNLOCK_KEYS(keys) PyMutex_Unlock(&keys->dk_mutex)
+
+#define ASSERT_KEYS_LOCKED(keys) assert(PyMutex_IsLocked(&keys->dk_mutex))
+#define LOAD_SHARED_KEY(key) _Py_atomic_load_ptr_acquire(&key)
+#define STORE_SHARED_KEY(key, value) _Py_atomic_store_ptr_release(&key, value)
+// Inc refs the keys object, giving the previous value
+#define INCREF_KEYS(dk)  _Py_atomic_add_ssize(&dk->dk_refcnt, 1)
+// Dec refs the keys object, giving the previous value
+#define DECREF_KEYS(dk)  _Py_atomic_add_ssize(&dk->dk_refcnt, -1)
+static inline void split_keys_entry_added(PyDictKeysObject *keys)
+{
+    ASSERT_KEYS_LOCKED(keys);
+
+    // We increase before we decrease so we never get too small of a value
+    // when we're racing with reads
+    _Py_atomic_store_ssize(&keys->dk_nentries, keys->dk_nentries + 1);
+    _Py_atomic_store_ssize(&keys->dk_usable, keys->dk_usable - 1);
review_comments.body:
We can use a weaker ordering here that will be faster, especially on x86 where "release" doesn't require any memory barrier:

```
    _Py_atomic_store_ssize_relaxed(&keys->dk_nentries, keys->dk_nentries + 1);
    _Py_atomic_store_ssize_release(&keys->dk_usable, keys->dk_usable - 1);
```

(I don't think we have `_Py_atomic_store_ssize_release` yet, though)

I find the memory orderings hard to reason correctly about, so I like to model them with [CDSChecker](https://plrg.ics.uci.edu/software_page/42-2/). Here's the model I used for this:
https://github.com/colesbury/c11-model-checker/blob/cpython-models/test/gh-112075.c

There's a behavioral change in the default build here that worries me and possibly a bug in both builds. Previously, we checked `a->ma_keys->dk_nentries` every iteration. That can be significant because `_Py_dict_lookup()` and `PyObject_RichCompareBool()` can modify the dict, including change the keys object.
I think it'd be helpful to assert that the keys are locked at the top of this function, especially because the `UNLOCK_KEYS()` is in a code path that's not normally executed.
I was a bit confused that `insert_into_dictkeys` only operates on split keys, but that predates your PR.

This can simply check that the dict does not have a split table. The `!unicode` check is redundant.

Additionally, I'd suggest moving the `DK_IS_UNICODE(mp->ma_keys)` check inside the body of `insert_combined_dict` and getting rid of the `unicode` argument. I was a bit confused as to whether that argument indicated a unicode-only table or a new unicode key.


```suggestion
        if (!_PyDict_HasSplitTable(mp)) {
```
Same here. Just `if (!_PyDict_HasSplitTable(mp)) {`
